entities.name: King Nan of Zhou
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
King Nan of Zhou, personal name Ji Yan (姬延), who reigned from 314 BCE until his death in 256 BCE, was the final sovereign of the Zhou dynasty, a foundational era in Chinese history. His reign, spanning an extraordinary fifty-nine years, was the longest in the Zhou dynasty and all of pre-imperial China, yet it paradoxically presided over the complete erosion of royal authority amidst the tumultuous Warring States period. He inherited a kingdom reduced to a mere ceremonial entity, with its once vast domain fractured into tiny, vulnerable enclaves, primarily centered around the capital of Chengzhou (modern-day Luoyang). His significance lies not in military prowess or political dominance, but as the poignant symbol of an ancient dynasty's protracted demise, marking the definitive transition towards imperial unification.

During his extended tenure, King Nan attempted to navigate the perilous geopolitical landscape by engaging in intricate diplomacy, often seeking to play the powerful states of Qin, Chu, Qi, Zhao, Han, Wei, and Yan against one another. Despite holding the revered title of 'Son of Heaven,' his actual power was negligible, his royal domain consisting of little more than the immediate capital and its surrounding towns. He famously tried to organize a 'Vertical Alliance' (Hezong) against the expansionist state of Qin, a strategy that ultimately proved ineffective against Qin's overwhelming military and administrative might. The Zhou royal house, already impoverished and politically marginalized, was finally extinguished when Qin armies seized the royal domain, effectively ending the dynasty.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: King Nan's reign, despite its length, marked the definitive end of the Zhou dynasty, an eight-century-long foundational period in Chinese history. His death directly preceded the Qin unification, fundamentally transforming Chinese political and social structures from feudalism to empire.
